source: Ventura and Brown (2024) Creativity as Search for Small, Interesting Programs
finding: Creativity-as-search is defined as a traversal function T that repeatedly picks an artifact from a space B until it hits a goal set G. The chance that blind search works is the density d=|G|/|B|. If d is near 1, search is easy and no creativity is needed. If d is near 0, only a clever strategy succeeds.
numbers: Tic-tac-toe: 765 states after symmetry, 138 terminal; d about 0.12 for a draw-or-better by random play for the first player. 3-letter words: 1340 of 17576 strings, d=0.076, so random search fails within h tries with probability 0.924^h.
quote: Placing marks randomly gives the starting player a 12% chance of a draw or better
limits: Argument is analytic, with no experiment. It treats creative value as 0/1 and equal to an optimisation score.
agent_relevance: The density d is a number our S3 search control could estimate by sampling. If valid answers are dense, plain sampling is enough. If sparse, the agent must use structure, not more samples.

source: Ventura and Brown (2024) Creativity as Search for Small, Interesting Programs (Library of Babel case)
finding: Scaling the same density argument to books makes blind search hopeless. Even the loose goal set 'books made only of valid English words' has near-zero density. So base-level search over artifacts cannot be the creative process in large domains.
numbers: Book of 410 pages x 40 lines x 80 chars. 5-letter word density about 0.001 (12972 of 26^5 = 11,881,376). Sentence density about 10^-60. Book density about 10^-655980.
limits: Conservative estimate by the authors, not measured. It is an argument about uniform random search, not about guided search.
agent_relevance: Warns that 'generate many and pick' does not scale by itself in a huge space. Guidance has to come from structure, memory of tried directions, or checks that prune.

source: Ventura and Brown (2024) Creativity as Search for Small, Interesting Programs (programs not objects)
finding: Proposal: creativity is a search for small programs that produce good artifacts, not a search for the artifacts. Good search programs are short in description but slow to run (algorithmic information theory). The space of search programs is itself searched at a meta level, which needs two evaluators: Eb for artifacts and Ea for search algorithms.
numbers: The set of orderings of B has |B|! members. Only countably many orderings are computable by Turing machines. No benchmark numbers.
quote: creativity isn't a direct search for artifacts, but it is instead a search for small programs that produce them
limits: Base-level evaluation is likely uncomputable, and the authors call the Mondol and Brown measures undecidable. No empirical test.
agent_relevance: Supports a design where the agent searches for a generator (a rule, template or program) that yields many candidates, then checks by running code. It also supports code, not the model, as the selector.

source: Ventura and Brown (2024) Creativity as Search for Small, Interesting Programs (against LLM models of creativity)
finding: The authors argue that a language model learns the distribution of its training data (Ritchie's inspiring set) and a smooth latent manifold, so it models non-creative output and may be a creative dead end by itself.
numbers: No numbers. Position argument.
limits: Claim is contested. Later LLM-plus-evaluator systems (FunSearch, AlphaEvolve) get new results by adding search and checks around the model.
agent_relevance: G8 and G5 fit this: the model is a proposer, and novelty must come from a loop with outside checks.

source: Nair et al. (2024) Creative Problem Solving in Large Language and Vision Models: What Would it Take? (arXiv 2405.01453)
finding: Position paper. It maps Boden's three types to ML. Exploratory creativity is closest to search: tree-of-thought, MCTS and beam search all search the output space of the model, but not the embedding space (the model's conceptual space). Combinational and transformational routes are less explored. The authors argue search alone is limited by the embedding dimensions.
numbers: Small test only: 5 core objects, 10 test sets each, 50 samples per model, 4 images per set; random pick gives about 30%.
quote: Exploratory approaches involve exploration within the conceptual or equivalently, the embedding space of the model, and most closely relates to
limits: Preliminary. The experiment is about object replacement, not search; the search link is argument only. The authors note existing search methods do not target creative problem solving.
agent_relevance: Says our S3 search control covers the exploratory part only. Reframing the problem (an operator) covers the transformational part, which search cannot reach.

source: Nair et al. (2024) Creative Problem Solving in Large Language and Vision Models (experiment)
finding: Models do well when the usual object is present and poorly when a creative substitute is needed. Adding object-affordance information to the prompt generally helped. Adding task information mostly hurt. Adding both did not clearly help.
numbers: Nominal group accuracy: CLIP-B-32 100%, CLIP-B-16 92%, CLIP-L-14 98%, CLIP-H-14-laion 98%, ViLT-B-32 68%, LLaVA 98%. Replacement group is lower; exact bars only in a figure (not read as numbers). Random about 30%.
limits: Tiny test set, image-choice task, 5 core objects only. Not a search experiment.
agent_relevance: Re-describing an object by its function (affordance) is a cheap reframing step. Extra task text can hurt, in line with G1 (no added steps without a signal).

source: Wiggins (2006) A preliminary framework for description, analysis and comparison of creative systems (Knowledge-Based Systems 19(7); also Searching for computational creativity, New Generation Computing 24(3))
finding: Formalises Boden's idea as the Creative Systems Framework: a universe of concepts, rule sets that define the conceptual space, a traversal rule that picks the next concept, and an evaluation rule. Exploratory creativity is search in the space. Transformational creativity is a search at a meta level over the rule sets themselves.
numbers: No empirical numbers (theory paper).
limits: NOT opened this session: full text was not reachable (PDF host unreachable, repository lacks full text). Description is from memory plus the Ventura and Brown paper, which cites it as the founding formalisation and calls it abstract, not operational.
agent_relevance: Gives vocabulary for S3: conceptual space (allowed moves), traversal (our search policy), evaluation (code checks). Meta-level change of rules matches reframing operators.

source: Boden (1990/2004) The Creative Mind: Myths and Mechanisms
finding: Three kinds of creativity: combinational, exploratory (explore a conceptual space and find ideas that fit it) and transformational (change the space so new ideas become possible). P-creative means new to the maker; H-creative means new in history.
numbers: No numbers (conceptual theory).
limits: NOT opened: only the Wikipedia summary and quotes inside the LLM papers were read. Wikipedia calls transformational creativity far rarer and says Boden guides the field more as an inspirational touchstone than as a technical framework.
agent_relevance: P-creativity is the right target for our agent: new relative to its own history. Checking 'new to the agent' is doable in code (compare to earlier attempts).

source: Newell, Shaw and Simon (1962/1959) The Processes of Creative Thinking (RAND P-1320)
finding: Argues that creative thinking needs no separate theory from problem solving when the problem is new and hard. Their four criteria: novelty and usefulness; rejecting ideas accepted before; intense, persistent effort; and clarifying a vague, ill-defined problem.
numbers: No numbers cited here.
limits: NOT opened: only a catalogue entry, a search summary and the Wikipedia page that cites the criteria were read.
agent_relevance: Supports the schema stance that search control, not a special creative module, is the core. Persistent effort maps to exploratory creativity.

source: Franceschelli and Musolesi (2025) On the Creativity of Large Language Models
finding: Applies Boden's three types to LLMs. Argues LLMs trained on a distribution can at most show combinational or exploratory creativity. Transformational creativity is not reachable by current training. RLHF and DPO make text less diverse.
numbers: No experiment. Introduces B-novelty (new to the beholder) as the likely source of apparent creativity.
quote: LLMs might at most express combinatorial or exploratory creativity.
limits: Position paper. The claim that RLHF lowers diversity cites other work (Kirk et al. 2024).
agent_relevance: If our model is aligned and low-diversity, search over its output space will cover a narrower region than a human might. Code-side diversity checks matter.

source: Franceschelli (2026) On the Creativity of AI Agents
finding: For agents, exploration of the conceptual space is shaped by the tools and actions chosen. Predetermined tools keep the agent inside the current conception of the domain. Tool creation could in theory change the space, but tools come from an LLM, so convention still limits them.
numbers: No numbers. Names three gaps, the first being that agents lack intrinsic motivation.
limits: Position paper.
agent_relevance: An agent that writes its own helper code (generators, checkers) widens the space it searches. Matches Ventura and Brown's 'search for programs'.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
finding: Treats problem solving as search over a tree of partial thoughts, with the model proposing and valuing states and BFS or DFS choosing. Chain-of-thought, self-consistency and self-refine are special cases of limited trees. This is the most cited LLM instance of exploratory search.
numbers: Game of 24 (GPT-4): IO 7.3%, CoT 4.0%, CoT-SC (k=100) 9.0%, IO best of 100 33%, CoT best of 100 49%, ToT b=1 45%, ToT b=5 74%.
limits: Game of 24 has a checkable goal and a clean decomposition. The gain depends on the model generating good thoughts: GPT-3.5 ToT reaches only 19%.
agent_relevance: Search with a code-checked goal beats the same number of independent samples (74% vs 49% for 100 CoT samples). Supports S3 over best-of-N when states can be checked.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts (creative writing task)
finding: On the open task of writing a coherent passage ending in 4 given sentences, ToT scored higher than IO or CoT by a GPT-4 judge and was preferred by humans over CoT. Iterative refine did well too.
numbers: 100 tasks. GPT-4 coherence score 1-10: IO 6.19, CoT 6.93, ToT 7.56; with refine IO 7.67, ToT 7.91. Humans preferred ToT over CoT in 41 of 100 pairs, CoT over ToT in 21, 38 similar. GPT-3.5: IO 4.47, ToT 6.62. Cost: ToT about 5x tokens ($0.32 vs $0.06 per case for IO).
limits: Metric is coherence from a model judge (std about 0.56 across 5 samples), not novelty. Judge is the same model family as the generator. Diversity not measured.
agent_relevance: Search helps coherence, not shown for novelty. Under G8 and G5 we must not use a model judge to claim novelty gains.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts (cost and generation vs evaluation)
finding: ToT cost on Game of 24 is about 5.5k completion tokens, near 100 CoT samples (6.7k), yet it wins. Swapping models showed the bottleneck is thought generation, not evaluation.
numbers: GPT-4 generate + GPT-3.5 evaluate: 64%. GPT-3.5 generate + GPT-4 evaluate: 31%. GPT-4 both: 74%. GPT-3.5 both: 19%.
limits: Single task. Costs are 2023 prices.
agent_relevance: At equal tokens, structured search can win (G7 test). A weaker, cheaper model may do evaluation if checks are in code.

source: Sel et al. (2023) Algorithm of Thoughts: Enhancing Exploration of Ideas in Large Language Models
finding: Puts the search path inside one prompt using worked algorithmic examples, so the model runs a depth-first search in a single pass. Matches ToT with far fewer queries.
numbers: Game of 24 (author reproduction): ToT b=5 69% with 109.1 queries; AoT 71% with 1 query. Mini-crosswords: ToT 46.5% with over 200 queries; AoT 52% with 2 queries.
limits: Author-run numbers differ from the ToT paper's 74%. Needs hand-written algorithm examples. A single pass cannot use outside checks mid-run.
agent_relevance: Query count is a cost the harness must count. A one-pass search is cheaper but gives no code checkpoints (G2, G3).

source: Franceschelli and Musolesi (2024) Creative Beam Search: LLM-as-a-Judge for Improving Response Generation (ICCC 2024, Llama 2 7B)
finding: Diverse beam search generates candidates, then the same model picks the most creative. Users preferred it to nucleus sampling more often, but about a quarter of pairs were too alike to tell.
numbers: 31 graduate students, 217 answers. Preferred: CBS 45%, standard 29%, same 26%. The model's self-pick matched the diverse-beam-search top choice 29% of the time vs 35.3% by chance.
limits: Small, informal, one 7B model, 256 tokens. The selector is the generating model (self-judging), which G5 and G8 forbid for final choice. No novelty or diversity metric.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence for model-as-selector. Self-pick agreed less than chance with the diversity ranking: the judge adds a separate signal, but its validity is not shown.

source: Romera-Paredes et al. (2024) FunSearch: Mathematical discoveries from program search with large language models (Nature)
finding: The model writes programs (a priority function), a code evaluator scores them, and an island-based evolutionary database feeds the best back into the prompt. It found new cap sets because the search is over short programs, not the sets.
numbers: Cap set in n=8: found 512 vs previous best 496. Capacity lower bound raised from 2.2180 to 2.2202 (an admissible-set route gave 2.2184 first). Online bin packing, fraction of excess bins: first fit 6.42% on OR1, best fit 5.81%, FunSearch 5.30%; Weibull instances 4.00% / 3.79% / 0.03%.
limits: Needs an automatic scoring function and a human-written skeleton. Used large parallel compute (15 samplers, 150 CPU evaluators).
agent_relevance: Direct empirical support for Ventura and Brown: search over programs with code evaluation works where object search fails. Fits S3 plus code-selected output (G5, G8).

source: Novikov et al. (2025) AlphaEvolve: A coding agent for scientific and algorithmic discovery
finding: Extends FunSearch to whole codebases with an LLM ensemble, a program database and automatic evaluators. Ablations (no evolution, no context in prompt, no meta-prompt evolution, small base LLM only, no full-file evolution) were run on tensor decomposition and kissing numbers.
numbers: 4x4 complex matrix multiplication with 48 scalar multiplications (first improvement in 56 years over Strassen in that setting). Over 50 open maths problems: matched best known in 75%, improved in 20%. Kissing number in 11 dimensions raised to 593. Fleet scheduling heuristic recovers on average 0.7% of Google compute.
limits: Ablation curves are in figures; exact values not read. Needs automatic evaluators, which many tasks lack. Vendor paper, not independently replicated here.
agent_relevance: The 'no evolution' ablation (same seed program fed repeatedly) is the control for reusing earlier attempts. Supports keeping history in S3.

source: Lehman et al. (2022) Evolution through Large Models (ELM)
finding: A code model acts as the mutation operator inside MAP-Elites (quality-diversity). From one seed program it fills a map of different working robots. The generated data then trains a model to output designs for new terrains.
numbers: Sodarace map of 1,728 niches; 3 runs per seed; each run 1,024,000 evaluations (2,000 iterations x 512 diffs); 300M-parameter diff model. Nearly all seeds filled the map; the Square seed filled it more slowly. The Radial seed scored high but exploited chaotic dynamics that overfit flat ground.
limits: Toy physics domain. The pretrained diff model was out of distribution until fine-tuned. A second fine-tuning round gave diminishing returns. Percent filled is only in a figure.
agent_relevance: A quality-diversity map gives a concrete 'cells visited' structure for S3. It also warns that a high score can be an exploit, so G3 held-out checks are needed. See subfield C04.06.

source: Si, Yang and Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas?
finding: Over-generate and rank: 4000 seed ideas per topic, dedupe, rank. Blind expert review judged AI ideas more novel than human ideas. But generation plateaus in diversity and model-based ranking is near chance.
numbers: Novelty 4.84 human (N=49), 5.64 AI, 5.81 AI plus human rerank (p<0.05). About 5% of 4000 ideas survive dedupe (200 per topic; cosine similarity above 0.8). Agreement with human ranking: GPT-4o direct 50.0, GPT-4o pairwise 45.0, Claude-3.5 direct 51.7, vs human-human 56.1.
limits: Ideas not executed; 79 reviewers; NLP prompt-based topics only. Feasibility slightly lower for AI ideas.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that blind sampling saturates (duplicates rise) and that a model judge cannot pick winners. Supports a code-side dedupe and archive (G4, G5, G8).

source: Si, Hashimoto and Yang (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap: Execution Outcomes of LLM-Generated versus Human Research Ideas
finding: When 43 experts executed randomly assigned human or AI ideas (over 100 hours each), AI ideas lost much more score after execution. The ideation-stage lead of AI ideas disappeared and flipped in sign, though not significantly.
numbers: Ideas: 19 human, 24 AI. Ideation scores novelty/excitement/effectiveness/overall: human 4.91/4.40/4.83/4.60, AI 5.78/5.65/6.00/5.38. After execution: human 4.90/4.48/4.78/3.97, AI 4.73/3.90/4.13/3.41. Score change: human -0.010/+0.078/-0.052; AI -1.049/-1.760/-1.879 (FDR p 0.025/0.001/0.003).
limits: Execution-stage differences between human and AI are not significant (p 0.175 to 0.586). Single LLM (Claude-3.5-Sonnet) idea generator, NLP topics.
agent_relevance: Search judged before running overstates quality. Only running the idea (G3, G8) shows true value.

source: Bhushan, Zhang and Wang (2026) Can LLM Agents Discover? Evaluating Creativity on ML Engineering Tasks (COLM 2026)
finding: Agents that search over code solutions (AIDE greedy tree, AIRA-Dojo greedy / MCTS / evolutionary) lose novelty relative to their own past solutions as runs progress. They are more novel than medal-winning humans but score lower.
numbers: 10 MLE-Bench tasks, 8-hour budget, up to 10 episodes, 8 runs per task for AIDE (GPT-5 and Qwen3-32B) and AIRA-MCTS. Strategic exploration was 75% of behaviours early and 25% late; bug fixing rose from 15% to over 50%. Per-episode change in impact vs P-creativity: human r=-0.111, AIDE GPT-5 r=-0.021. All three AIRA strategies fell below P-creativity 1 within a few episodes.
limits: Judge is an LLM (validated against human ratings). The search-strategy comparison used 3 tasks and Qwen3-32B only. Authors say search strategy alone does not decide creativity or impact.
agent_relevance: Agents drift from exploring to exploiting. A code-side budget for exploration steps, tied to a signal, could slow that (G1).

source: Hu et al. (2024) Nova: An Iterative Planning and Search Approach to Enhance Novelty and Diversity of LLM Generated Ideas
finding: Planning what to retrieve next, then retrieving, raised the number of unique ideas over iterations. Without planning, uniqueness stopped growing after step 2.
numbers: Unique novel ideas 3.4 times the baseline (abstract). Ablation: no planning: 42.4 unique at step 2, 44.1 at step 3. No planning and no retrieval: 25.3, then 30.6, then 31.35. Human eval: Nova supplied 37.5% of top-4 ideas and 17.53% of worst-4.
limits: Uniqueness is judged by the authors' own pipeline. Not independently replicated. Idea ranking uses a model.
agent_relevance: Directed expansion that brings in new outside material beats resampling. Maps to a search step that adds a new source, not a new sample.

source: Tian et al. (2025) MacGyver: Are Large Language Models Creative Problem Solvers?
finding: On 1,600+ problems that need unusual use of objects, GPT-4 is often wrong in physically infeasible ways. Humans are bimodal, LLMs middling. Prompts that mix divergent and convergent thinking helped.
numbers: GPT-4: 18.9% efficient solution, 37.5% infeasible. Majority correctness: humans 79.3% vs GPT-4 73.3%. Error types: wrong tool usage 42.4%, goal not achieved 17.7%, unfaithful to constraints 16.9%, unavailable tools 9.5%.
limits: Judging of solutions is partly by models plus human checks; problems are generated automatically.
agent_relevance: A cheap physical or logical constraint check after each proposal removes infeasible ideas (G2). Supports doubt on a signal, not on a schedule.

source: Velardo and Vallati (2016) A General Framework for Describing Creative Agents
finding: Extends Wiggins to a formal agent: artefact space, a generation operator limited by constraints, an evaluation operator with memory (to judge novelty and secure P-creativity), and an optional update operator that can change generation and evaluation (the route to transformational creativity).
numbers: No numbers. Pure formalism.
limits: Not tested on any system. The authors present it as a description tool.
agent_relevance: Clean mapping: generation = proposer, evaluation with memory = code-side novelty check, update = operators that alter the search rules.

source: Ritchie (2007) Some empirical criteria for attributing creativity to a computer program (Minds and Machines)
finding: Proposes testable criteria built from typicality and quality of the outputs and from how outputs relate to the program's inspiring set (the examples it was built from). Ventura and Brown reuse the inspiring-set idea against LLMs.
numbers: No numbers recalled with confidence; the count of criteria was not verified.
limits: NOT opened. Known only through citation in Ventura and Brown (the url is the citing paper) and from memory.
agent_relevance: The inspiring-set check is a code test: compare new ideas with the set already seen or supplied, and call a near copy not new.
